1.pericope_label: Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars
debates: Whether the vine is empty, emptying, plundered or luxuriant
Why the increase of fruit produced an increase of altars
What bringing forth fruit unto himself means
outliers: Ellicott rejects the received rendering as inconsistent with the rest of the verse and reads the vine as luxuriant, building on it a history of the northern kingdom prosperity
Calvin holds that those who make the word mean empty are mistaken, since the verb properly means to plunder, so that the vine is one robbed after the vintage
themes: A vine that casts its grapes before they are ripe
Costlier images bought with a richer harvest
A tree of all others least serviceable if it bears nothing
Mercies credited to the idol that did not send them

2.pericope_label: Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty: he shall break down their altars, he shall spoil their images
debates: From what the heart is divided
When the people said they had no king
What covenant the false swearing broke
outliers: Ellicott reports that modern expositors abandon the received rendering of the divided heart for a treacherous or smooth one, against the ancient versions and the Jewish commentators
Calvin prefers the reading by which the people freely professed to be the most faithful worshippers, rather than the one making them follow their own counsels daringly
themes: A wife whose affection is divided from her husband
A king who could not help because he was a captive too
Judgment springing up like a poisonous weed in the furrows
Words that were nothing but words

5.pericope_label: It shall be also carried unto Assyria for a present to king Jareb: Ephraim shall receive shame
debates: Whether the verb means to fear, to be banished, or to worship
Who carried the calf away and why
What the figure for the doomed king properly means
outliers: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both abandon the rendering foam for a chip or splinter on the water, making the king a helpless fragment rather than a scum
Clarke proposes reading howled for rejoiced, admitting that no manuscript yet discovered supports it and resting the change on the necessity of the place
themes: A feminine plural used to make an idol ridiculous
Worshippers weeping over the deportation of their own god
Gods who need help from mortals rather than giving it
Foam that rides high on the water and is only its excrement

8.pericope_label: The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars
debates: Why the place is called by a name of iniquity
What the thorn and thistle signify
How far the cry to the mountains reaches
outliers: Calvin explains the change of name as an answer to those who defended the shrine by appealing to a patriarchal vision, holding that a corrupted worship cannot be covered by an honourable title
Clarke reports a judgment that the parallelism here is finer than the parallel passages in the later Scriptures, and that one earlier prophet wants its dramatic form
themes: A house of God renamed a house of iniquity
A strong hammer needed because the hearts were iron
Thorn and thistle from the first curse growing on an altar
Men who would rather have a hill fall on them than face what is coming

9.pericope_label: O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah: there they stood: the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity did not overtake them
debates: Which event at Gibeah is meant
Whether the sin is the same as that of old or greater
Whether the last clause is a question or a statement
outliers: Ellicott renders the last clause as a question expecting yes, that the war against the wicked shall overtake them, and reports and rejects the categorical reading Pusey and others prefer

Calvin answers the objection that the people avenged the crime by observing that those who execute the vengeance of God are often no better, citing a king called a robber for the vengeance he carried out
themes: A crime of the judges reenacted as a copy from its original
A continuous rope of iniquity spun from one age to the next
Malefactors who won the first two battles and lost the third
Six hundred men who escaped a war that has not yet caught up with them

10.pericope_label: And Ephraim is as an heifer that is taught, and loveth to tread out the corn; but I passed over upon her fair neck
debates: How God can be said to desire to chastise
What the two furrows or two iniquities are
Why the heifer prefers threshing to ploughing
outliers: Calvin answers the objection that this verse contradicts others where God grieves at punishing, holding that passions do not belong to God and that both are characters put on in condescension to human capacity
Ellicott allows that the threshing may stand for the rough treatment this people dealt its neighbours, but prefers the reading that makes it easy work and self-indulgence
themes: A heifer that eats while it works because the law forbids muzzling it
Nations stirred to war by a hiss or a nod
A people who liked the fruit of work better than the work
A fair neck brought under a yoke to end its self-indulgence

12.pericope_label: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the Lord
debates: Whether the call to sow is an exhortation or a protest
What seed is to be sown
Whether the word rendered thy way should be read thy chariots
outliers: Calvin denies that this is a simple exhortation and takes it as a protestation that God had laboured in vain, reading the following verse as the reason for the charge
Ellicott reports a variant giving chariots for way, followed by the Greek and several modern scholars, but allows that the received text yields a fine meaning
themes: Fallow ground that must be broken before any seed will take
A season passing while the seed is still in the sack
A rift in a storm-cloud showing the light behind it
Men who ate the fruit of their own lies

14.pericope_label: So shall Beth-el do unto you because of your great wickedness: in a morning shall the king of Israel utterly be cut off
debates: What historical slaughter the comparison refers to
Why the shrine rather than God is named as doing the evil
What the morning signifies
outliers: Clarke declares the history behind the comparison simply unknown and conjecture useless, where Ellicott canvasses three scholarly theories and rejects one as far-fetched
Calvin explains the construction as deliberate, since naming the shrine rather than God shows that the cause of the evil lay in the people themselves
themes: A tumult that rises on every side in one moment
A mother dashed in pieces upon her children in a remembered battle
A shrine named as the author of the ruin it caused
A king cut off in the early morning, leaving neither root nor branch
